seen.where: Newberry Digital Collections / CARLI nby_graff 16330-16333 (Burr letter, Graff *502), viewed via the Wikimedia Commons copies 'Aaron Burr letter to James Wilkinson, 1806 (NBY 16330-16333).jpg'; Wilkinson affidavit NBY 16324-16325 (Graff 4668 memorandum); collections.newberry.org/archive/-2KXJ8ZSSB3NK5.html
seen.extent: One 4-page autograph-in-secretary's-hand letter, page 1 viewed in full: about 17 lines of numbers 'page.line' plus dotted/barred forms and hieroglyph signs; the dorse is endorsed 'Burr Letter 22d July by Swartwout'.
seen.cipher: Dictionary code (number pairs, with superscript/overline marks and symbol 'hieroglyphs'); the leaf opens 'Your letter post marked 13th May is received. I have at length 263.13...' which is the opening of the famous Burr-Wilkinson cipher letter of July 1806, in the copy Wilkinson received via Swartwout. Wilkinson's separate sheet (16324) is a sworn statement that the numbers and hieroglyphs were written by Capt. Campbell Smith in 1794-96, not a key; no decipherment is written on the cipher page.

prior_art.decode: Not on DECODE (no Burr/Wilkinson Newberry record in the repo DECODE list; known.py 'Graff f*502' and 'Burr Wilkinson' hit only this entry).
prior_art.tomokiyo: Burr cipher letter is covered on Tomokiyo-style lists as a dictionary code (Entick); no new reading of this copy needed. Search 'Burr Wilkinson cipher letter 1806' gave only the standard accounts.
prior_art.lasry: Lasry's dictionary-code work (Dahlke/Lasry-Kopal 'Solving historical dictionary codes', arXiv 2010.04746) concerns Wilkinson's Spanish correspondence, not this letter.
prior_art.edition: Wilkinson's deciphered text was put in evidence at Burr's trial (Richmond 1807, Robertson's Report; famous-trials.com/burr/162-letter reproduces 'as interpreted by General Wilkinson'); Jefferson Papers (founders.archives.gov) and Madison Papers editors discuss the copy and its alterations.
prior_art.literature: Kahn, 'Masked Dispatches' ch. 13 (NSA) on the Burr cipher letter; Entick's dictionary key described by Easton 1807 (Jefferson Papers); searches: Burr cipher letter decipherment/Entick, Newberry Graff 502, trial 1807 text.

vetting.key_check: The key is a pocket dictionary (Entick, paged alike by Burr and Wilkinson); not held in the repo, but the plaintext is printed (trial text as interpreted by Wilkinson), so a reading exists and nothing is left to find with a key.
vetting.duplicates: known.py (Graff f*502, Burr Wilkinson): no other repo entry; related Wilkinson entries 482 and 761 are other letters. The famous letter is the same text as this leaf; the Newberry sheet is Wilkinson's received copy, not a new variant.
vetting.closed: This Newberry leaf is the famous Burr cipher letter of 22 July 1806 (Wilkinson's received copy, endorsed 'by Swartwout'); Wilkinson's decipherment was printed at the 1807 trial. Remaining question is only comparing the leaf with the printed text.

seen.extent: One sheet, a block of about 39 columns by 41 rows of invented stroke signs (about 1,600), three title lines of signs above, and a printed-style footer 'DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE ... COPYRIGHT 1925' signed William H. Conklin
seen.cipher: Hand-drawn invented glyphs built from a vertical stem with hooks and bars, about 40 columns wide, with the footer stating the plaintext and the symbol count; no key, grid legend or decipherment appears on the sheet. A sign-per-word code is the likely system (the post's commenter Gerd notes sign count is close to the word count).

prior_art.decode: Not on DECODE (known.py 'Conklin' hits only the catalogue; no DECODE record).
prior_art.tomokiyo: No cryptiana entry for Conklin; search 'Conklin cryptogram Declaration of Independence' found nothing.
prior_art.lasry: George Lasry commented on the Cipherbrain thread (about the Kruh collection) but no solution; no Lasry paper on it.
prior_art.edition: Not published; Kruh listing 'Conklin, Dr. W.H. The Conklin Cryptogram. A True Cipher. Two Xerox pages plus Conklin letter and other material' (National Cryptologic Museum, Kruh collection) may hold his own explanation; LoC Fabyan collection has his 'The code word'.
prior_art.literature: Searches: Cipherbrain post and 15 comments; 'Conklin Cryptogram A True Cipher'; 'C.C. characters Conklin Riverbank NYPL solved'; Kruh collection. No decipherment found; note Friedmans had left Riverbank by 1925 (commenter), so 'Riverbank file' only means the NYPL collection.

vetting.key_check: Plaintext is the Declaration of Independence with the 56 signers (1,339 words); the Declaration text can be set against the 1,636-sign count as a known-plaintext test. No existing key is held; none of the repo's keys applies to an invented 1925 glyph code.
vetting.duplicates: known.py 'Conklin' and 'MssCol 176': only this entry and the Riverbank boxes entry (851); no other copy digitised (Kruh copy is Xerox, not online).

851.unvetted: Box-level archive description only ('student exercises and lessons, Mexican codes'; 'unsorted material concerning cryptography'); nothing shows ciphertext. archives.nypl.org/mss/176 is behind an Imperva CAPTCHA (not clicked) and the Wayback copy of the box list renders blank in Chrome; curl of the NSA blog PDF returns 403. The NSA historians' account recorded in the entry says the nine Riverbank boxes were 'very duplicative and mixed' with no cipher intercepts, so a verdict needs the reading-room list, not a guess.

852.unvetted: Finding aid (ICU.SPCL.HARPERSN.pdf, read: Series VI, Box 61 f.19 'Memoranda on translations and code messages found with the Sisson documents (1918-1920)') gives no ciphertext, only a memoranda folder that is not online; Sisson documents prior art (Harper-Jameson study, CPI pamphlet October 1918 printing the Petrograd-Brest-Litovsk telegram transcripts, Kennan 1956) means any code messages were handled and translated at the time, but I could not establish what the folder holds. Needs the folder (U Chicago Special Collections) or the CPI pamphlet appendix compared.

seen.extent: Volume 19[3 holds about 50 pages in Geheimschrift (catalogue no. 23: 'Rezepte und Briefe an Landgraf Moritz in Geheimschrift', ff. 62r-62v illustrated). Seen: image 150 (f. 70v), an invented runic-style glyph script in 5 lines with a tipped-in slip carrying a symbol/letter table; ff. 62r-62v are clear German numbered points.
seen.cipher: Invented-alphabet Geheimschrift (letter substitution with a key slip and key lists in the volume, 'Schluessel zu zwei Geheimschriften' per the catalogue); partly published by Schmitz/Winkelmann 1961. No decipherment of the glyph leaves is written on them. The frame check of 30 Oct found the linked volume without a cipher page: that volume is in fact the right one (the record's annotation names theol. 181 as its former cover and Ms. chem. 19[2/[5 as the Popp letters).

prior_art.decode: Not on DECODE (known.py 'chem. 19' and 'Moritz Popp': only this entry and the Europeana sweep).

vetting.closed: Schmitz/Winkelmann 1961 published part of the Geheimschrift pieces and the volume carries its own key material; the rest needs the 1961 table or a rebuild from the in-volume keys.

seen.cipher: TNA description of /59: 'Folio 118. Undecyphered paper.'; /47 (f. 94, 23 Nov 1723): 'Received from Mr Willes and Mr Ashfield. They say this cannot be decyphered without vast trouble and time unless they had more of it'. So the entry's 'several enclosed cipher papers' overstates it: the surviving cipher text is the one undecyphered paper.
